parts.title: The art of bargaining
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My first trip to a market abroad was a lesson I will never forget. I was in Morocco, and I saw a beautiful brass lamp. The seller said, "Fifty euros, my friend." That seemed a fair price, so I put my hand in my pocket.

Suddenly, a local man standing nearby said quietly, "Never accept the first price. Offer half." I was embarrassed, but I tried. "Twenty-five," I said. The seller looked shocked and put his hand on his heart. "My family will go hungry!" he said. I smiled. The man next to me whispered that it was part of the game.

We went back and forth for ten minutes. The seller dropped his price to forty, then thirty-five, while I increased mine to thirty. In the end, we agreed on thirty-two euros and shook hands. Then he gave me a glass of mint tea, and we talked about football for half an hour.

Later, my guide told me that the real price was probably twenty. I did not mind. I had learned something, made a new friend and bought a lamp that still stands in my living room.

questions.explanation: The seller asked fifty euros.

questions.explanation: He said never accept the first price and offer half.

questions.explanation: He acted shocked and said his family would go hungry, but it was part of the game.

questions.explanation: She did not mind; she had learned something and made a friend.

parts.title: The oldest markets in the world
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Markets are older than shops. [1] Long before there were coins, people met in open places to swap food, tools and cloth.

In ancient cities, markets were often the busiest and loudest place in town. [2] Crowds of people came from the villages to sell their goods and to hear the news.

In the Middle Ages, European towns held weekly market days. [3] The law said that nobody was allowed to sell goods outside the market square.

Some markets became famous across the world. [4] The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul has over four thousand shops, and some of them have been owned by the same family for centuries.

Today, many people buy online, but markets are still popular. [5] They offer something that a website cannot: a chance to touch, smell and taste before you buy.
sentences: Nobody knows when the first one began.
Many people say they prefer the lively atmosphere.
Their prices were fixed by the king.
Millions of visitors go to see them every year.
Everyone brought their own bags and baskets.
Each town had its own rules.
People like to meet and talk as well as shop.

gaps.explanation: Nobody knows when the first market began; the next sentence says people met before coins.
People liked to meet and talk; the next sentence says crowds came from the villages.
Each town had its own rules; the next sentence says nobody could sell outside the square.
Millions of visitors go to see them; the next sentence gives the Grand Bazaar as an example.
Many people prefer the lively atmosphere; the next sentence says markets offer touch, smell and taste.

parts.title: Buying second-hand
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Buying second-hand clothes or furniture is a good way to save money and to help the planet. When you buy something that someone else has used, you give it [1] new life and reduce waste. Markets and charity shops are great places to look. Always check the item carefully [2] you pay for it. Look for holes, stains or broken parts. Smell it, too, because bad smells are hard to remove. Do not be afraid to ask for a lower price, as sellers [3] expect it. If the object is electrical, ask the seller to show you that it works. For clothes, try them on if you can, because sizes are different in every country. [4] you cannot try them on, measure them with a tape. Finally, wash everything carefully when you get home. parts.title: A message from the market manager
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: manager
turns.text: Good morning, traders and visitors. This is Enoch, the market manager, with some news about changes at Riverside Market. First, the opening time. Many of you told me that seven is too early on the cold winter days, and some people wanted nine. After a long meeting, we have decided on eight. That’s a small change, but I hope it helps the traders. Second, the days. At the moment we are open on Wednesdays and Saturdays. A new day will be added, but not Sunday, because the council said no. From next month we will also open on Fridays, because lots of people finish work early then. Third, the food court. We have always had eight food stalls, and next month there will be twelve. That’s four new stalls, with food from Turkey, Mexico and Nigeria. The new area will be in the old car park, next to the main gate. Fourth, music. We’ll have live musicians every Saturday. People asked for them in the square, and we thought of using the roof of the town hall, but that is too dangerous. So there will be a small stage in the middle of the square, next to the fountain. Fifth, the fees. Because we are spending money on all this, stall owners must pay a little more each week. I was going to ask for ten pounds extra, which seemed too much, so after talking to many traders we agreed on five pounds. Last of all, our green plan. From the first of June we will not give out plastic bags. You can bring your own bag, or buy a cloth one. They were going to cost two pounds, but in the end we chose a cheaper price, just one pound. Remember, you can read all the details on the notice board by the main gate. Thank you for listening, and have a great week.

gaps.explanation: Seven was too early and nine was suggested, but the meeting decided on eight.

gaps.prompt: An extra market day will be ___
gaps.explanation: The market is open on Wednesdays and Saturdays; Sunday was refused, and the new day will be Friday.

parts.title: An interview with a market trader
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Pike, you’ve worked at this market for thirty years. What do you love most about it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Well, people think it must be the money, but honestly it’s not great, and some weeks I earn very little. The fresh air is nice, though in winter it’s freezing. No, it’s the customers. I know their names, their children’s names, even their dogs’ names. Some of them have been buying from me for twenty years, and we’ve shared so many stories. That’s what keeps me coming back every morning.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Your day starts very early, doesn’t it? Why is that?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Three in the morning, yes. People think I need to avoid the traffic, but at that hour there’s no traffic anyway, and I’ve no garden to look after, because my vegetables come from the farm. I go to the wholesale market so that I can choose the best vegetables before the restaurants buy them. If you arrive late, you get what’s left. After that I drive to the stall and set up.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What about bad weather? How do you feel about it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Oh, I’ve seen everything: rain, snow, wind that blew my umbrella away. I used to be furious when it happened, and I did lose money on some days. I’m not scared of it, though, and I don’t worry about it any more. It’s part of the job, so I put on three jackets and I carry on. A customer in the rain is a special customer, and they like it that I’m there.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tell me about your carrots. People say they are famous.

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Ha, they are! They’re not cheaper than the supermarket ones, in fact they cost a bit more. And they aren’t pretty either, because some are crooked and some are small. But when you taste one, you understand. They come from soil that the farmer has looked after for forty years. Nobody forgets that flavour, especially children.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to somebody who starts a stall today?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Don’t copy the supermarkets, you’ll never win that game. Working longer hours won’t help, you’ll just be tired, and I tried that for a year. Just tell the truth about what you sell and smile, even on a bad day. If a tomato isn’t good, say so. People remember that, and they come back.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And finally, who will take over the stall one day, and why are you happy about it?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My daughter, Mia. She didn’t study business, she studied art, and I don’t think she’ll earn a lot at first. But she has stood next to me every Saturday since she was eight, so she knows every customer and every trick. I’m sure she’ll do it better than me. I’ll retire happily.

questions.prompt: What does Pike enjoy most about the market?
questions.explanation: The money is not great and the air is cold in winter; what he loves is knowing the customers and their stories.

questions.prompt: Why does Pike get up so early?

questions.prompt: What does Pike say about his carrots?
questions.explanation: They cost a bit more and some are crooked, but the taste is something nobody forgets.

questions.prompt: What is Pike's advice for new traders?
questions.explanation: Copying supermarkets and working longer hours do not work; he tells them to tell the truth and smile.

questions.prompt: Why is Pike happy that his daughter will take over?
options: She has helped him for years
She will earn more than he does
questions.explanation: She did not study business and she will not earn much at first, but she has stood next to him every Saturday since she was eight.
